newsitem.title: FRANCE: French railroad set to to enter telecoms field.
newsitem.headline: French railroad set to to enter telecoms field.

text.p: French loss-making state railways SNCF is set to decide on Thursday whether to plunge headlong into the telecommunications sector ahead of the 1998 liberalisation of the field, rivaling France Telecom.

A spokesman for the Societe Nationale des Chemins de Fer (SNCF) said the railroad's supervisory board, meeting on Thursday, would discuss a possible increase in the share capital of its telecoms unit Telecom Developpement.
He had no comment on a report in the La Tribune Desfosses newspaper saying the increase, of some 930 million French francs ($181.5 million) would take the capital to 2.07 billion francs.

On top of that, there would be the transfer of 1.07 billion francs in intangible assets representing the unit's right to use space in SNCF stations and the capacity of SNCF's existing telecommunications cable network.
The paper added that banks Compagnie Financiere de Paribas and the Caisse des Depots could take a 550 million franc stake in the unit.
At Paribas, which is advising Italian railroads Ferrovie dello Stato (FS) in the privatisation of its Telesistemi unit, there was no immediate comment on the report.
At Caisse des Depots et de Consignations, a state bank, nobody was immediately available for comment.
The SNCF has France's second-biggest fibre optic telecommunications network, behind France Telecom, and has received the right to operate an "alternative infrastructure network."

As part of the gradual liberalisation of French telecommunications, culminating in full market liberalisation in 1998 and partial privatisation of France Telecom in spring 1997, the SNCF is already renting its capacity to mobile telecommunications operators. From 1998, it could also do so to operators of fixed networks.
To commercially run its network, the SNCF has opened a tender in which it is being advised by U.S. investment bank Lehman Brothers.
La Tribune said Generale des Eaux, Lyonnaise des Eaux as well as Bouygues were among the candidates.

Generale des Eaux, through its new unit Cegetel and possibly in alliance with AT&T, has the ambition to become France's second-biggest telecommunications operator. Its SFR unit already uses SNCF line capacity for its mobile network.
Bouygues, a building group with media interests, is the third and last arrival in the mobile telecoms market while Lyonnaise des Eaux has not yet unveiled its telecoms strategy.

The two utilities, Generale and Lyonnaise, both have cable television networks which can also be used in an alternative network. Another big owner of such a private network, apart from the military, is electricity utility EDF and gas group GDF.
La Tribune said with the arrival of an operator, the capital of Telecom Developpement could rise to 4.5 billion francs.
Under that scenario, it could expand its network over five years to 12,000 kms (7,500 miles) from 8,700 kms now. The unit is expected to become profitable in 2001/2002.
All European railroad companies have such networks, used to link stations and signposts and running along the railtracks.
SNCF has joined the Hermes venture which will link all these networks in Europe. ($1=5.124 French Franc)
